title: Solene Atelier devotional pendant collection: neutralise a six-piece two-session shot batch to one house white point against an in-frame grey card, match the red-stone pieces to one house garnet, isolate each onto white, vectorise the hallmark, and data-merge one spec card per piece
grounding_note: Adapted from a real Upwork brief in which a jeweler had finished a custom Sterling Silver 925 pendant (opening double doors on hidden hinges, a red stone as the locking element, Islamic geometric openwork, and Arabic calligraphy engraving) and asked a freelancer to help present and market the piece and to 'share similar work, estimated cost, and timeline.' The real brief's literal first ask is a 3D CAD model (.3DM/STL), which the Adobe connector explicitly CANNOT author (3D/CAD/STL are not-available), so the deliverable is honestly re-anchored, within the identical jewelry_photo category and the Nonprofit/Religious/Community vertical, onto what the connector CAN do to help the maker 'share similar work' with an estimate: turn the maker's own studio photographs of the finished pieces into a color-consistent product-photo set plus a data-merged lookbook / spec-and-estimate sheet. The client and the studio are laundered to a FICTIONAL bespoke devotional-jewelry house, 'Solene Atelier' (owner an unnamed silversmith); the six piece names (Meridian locket, Reed pendant, Ember signet, Cove pendant, Vale pendant, Halo pendant) and all copy are fictional. Materials (Sterling Silver 925, garnet, carnelian, turquoise, oxidised silver, bronze) and motifs (Islamic geometric openwork, Arabic calligraphy) are generic. ENRICHMENT required to make the chain concrete, failable and measurable: instead of one hero, the atelier shot its SIX signature pieces across TWO sessions under mismatched light and clipped a photographic 18% neutral grey card into the corner of every frame (standard tethered-shoot practice) so white balance can be reconciled after the fact; the pieces were laid on a seamless WHITE sweep so a connector-legal knockout onto solid white is possible. CONNECTOR CONSTRAINT honoured explicitly: image_remove_background isolates only the OUTER background and cannot punch an ENCLOSED interior hole (the openwork filigree cells, the closed bail loop) transparent — because the pieces sit on a white sweep, those enclosed cells are captured against white and simply read white after the outer knockout, which is exactly the clean-white PDP result wanted, so the workflow never claims a see-through interior cut-out (which the tool cannot produce) as an acceptance gate. The vector hallmark comes from a supplied flat inked maker's-mark scan (not the photographic engraving) so image_vectorize traces clean edges. No layout is composed from scratch: the lookbook spec cards are produced by data-merging a genuinely hand-authored InDesign template. No real person, brand, org, product, marketplace, standard or trademark is named anywhere; only Upwork (source platform) and Adobe/InDesign (the platform) appear.
one_line_ask: Take Solene Atelier's six devotional-pendant photos shot across two mismatched lighting sessions (each with a grey reference card in frame), neutralise every frame to the card so the whole collection shares one house white point and the polished silver reads true, bring the red-stone pieces to one matched house garnet without killing the facet sparkle, isolate each piece onto a clean solid-white PDP background with its openwork intact, vectorise the atelier hallmark, and data-merge the authored InDesign template to produce one press-ready spec-and-estimate card per piece.
full_brief:
Solene Atelier makes bespoke devotional jewelry to order, and we are putting together a presentation set and a spec-and-estimate lookbook so we can show new clients 'similar work' with a price and a lead time on each piece. We are NOT reshooting. We are handing you six photographs — our whole signature collection, one shot per piece, each laid on a white sweep with a small 18% grey reference card in the corner of the frame. Here is the problem: they were shot over two sessions on different days under different light — some under cool daylight from the workshop window, some under warm tungsten bench lamps, one or two off-level, one dark, one bright — so straight out of the folder the collection looks like a jumble and the silver reads a different colour from piece to piece. A set that mismatched reads cheap next to work this fine.

What we need on the photos: bring every image to a consistent, true look by neutralising each one to the grey card it carries — in your finished frame that card must read a clean neutral grey (equal across the channels), and once every card is neutral the whole collection will sit at one shared house white point with the sterling silver reading as true bright silver, not warm or blue. When you are done, tell us the final white-balance and exposure settings you landed on for each frame so we can confirm the set was matched to one point rather than eyeballed. Above all, every piece must stay true to its own materials — nothing pushed off its real colour, the deepest darks staying rich and detailed rather than crushed to black or washed to grey, and the brightest polished metal holding its highlight detail without clipping out — so the collection reads as one cohesive, true-to-life set.

Second, a colour-truth pass: several of the pieces are set with a red stone, and across the two sessions those reds have drifted apart. Bring every red stone to ONE deep, rich house garnet — a true, deep jewel-red in the same colour family, just deepened and settled, not a jump to some far-off hue — and it has to sit under the real facets, sparkle and shadow of the cut stone, no flat painted-on colour and nothing that bleeds onto the silver or the sweep. Leave the other stones (a turquoise, a clear stone) their true colour; only the reds are being matched.

Third, build the marketplace packshots: lift each piece cleanly off its sweep and set it on a pure solid-white background with the sweep and the grey card gone, hair-fine chain and openwork edges looking natural, no halo — and the open filigree cells and the bail loop must read clean, not bricked in with a solid slab of colour. Fourth, our maker's hallmark only exists as a flat inked scan on off-white card — get it clean and razor-sharp as vector art for the cards and future stamping. Finally, build the lookbook: we have hand-built the InDesign spec-card template with the real placeholder fields and two image slots (one for the piece's packshot, one for the hallmark at the top of the card), and we are giving you the roster with each piece's name, materials, stone, mechanism, motif, our estimated price and our lead time; merge them so every piece gets its own single-page card with its copy bound verbatim, its matched packshot dropped in, and the crisp hallmark in the masthead, then hand back one press-ready ~300 DPI card per piece as a single lookbook PDF (one page per piece, the Meridian locket first) plus a web JPEG we can email. Bind our copy and our prices exactly as written — do not rewrite them. Acceptance: every grey card neutral and the whole set matched to one white point; every red stone on the one house garnet with its facets intact; each piece isolated on clean white with its openwork preserved; the hallmark a crisp vector; and exactly one finished card per roster row.

inputs.name: meridian_locket_flatlay.jpg
inputs.gen_prompt: Photoreal top-down studio product photograph of an ornate closed Sterling Silver 925 book/door locket pendant on a fine silver chain, laid flat on a seamless white paper sweep. Intricate Islamic geometric openwork filigree across the face with genuine see-through cells showing the white sweep beneath, fine engraved Arabic calligraphy across the doors, a small faceted deep-red ruby set as the central locking clasp, a closed bail loop at the top where the chain passes. A standard 18% neutral grey card and a small white swatch sit flat on the sweep at the lower-left edge of frame. Shot under COOL overcast workshop-window daylight with a distinct blue cast, slightly under-exposed and flat, the whole frame tilted about 4 degrees as if shot quickly on a copy stand. Real polished-silver micro-scratches, faint fingerprints and specular glints, soft contact shadow. Straight off the camera, un-graded, not CGI-glossy. ~4200 px long edge.
inputs.realism_notes: Piece 1 / the hero (Meridian locket), Session A (cool/blue, slightly under, tilted ~4deg). Carries a RED ruby that must be matched to the shared house garnet target, so this frame both establishes the house white point AND is one of the red-match pair. The openwork cells and the closed bail show the WHITE sweep, so after the outer background knockout they read clean white with no interior punch needed (the connector cannot punch an enclosed hole transparent, and here it does not have to). Grey card in frame is the neutralisation ground truth; it sits far-left so it can be neutralised first and then cropped out when the packshot is framed on the piece. Real metal micro-detail keeps it photographic and gives auto_straighten genuine work.

inputs.name: reed_pendant_flatlay.jpg
inputs.gen_prompt: Photoreal top-down studio product photograph of a Sterling Silver 925 teardrop pendant on a fine chain, laid flat on a seamless white paper sweep, a faceted deep-red garnet cabochon set at its centre, delicate Islamic geometric openwork border with genuine see-through cells over the white sweep, a closed bail at the top. A standard 18% neutral grey card and a small white swatch sit on the sweep at the lower-right edge. Shot under WARM tungsten bench-lamp light with a strong orange cast and a slightly bright exposure, level. Real brushed-and-polished silver texture, tiny tool marks, soft contact shadow. Un-graded catalog shot, not CGI. ~4200 px long edge.
inputs.realism_notes: Piece 2 (Reed pendant), Session B (warm/orange, slightly bright, level). The SECOND red-stone piece: its garnet under the warm cast drifts brighter/oranger than piece 1's ruby, so the two must be driven to ONE identical house garnet across the two sessions — the measurable colour-match core. Its neutralisation move is the OPPOSITE sign to piece 1 (cool it, pull exposure down), so a single shared white balance across the batch cannot serve both — the identical-params trap. Openwork and bail on white sweep read white after knockout.

inputs.name: ember_signet_flatlay.jpg
inputs.gen_prompt: Photoreal top-down studio product photograph of a warm bronze devotional signet pendant on a leather-and-silver cord, laid flat on a seamless white paper sweep, an oval amber carnelian cabochon set in the face, a pierced geometric border with see-through cells over the white sweep, a closed bail. A standard 18% neutral grey card and a small white swatch sit on the sweep at the frame edge. Shot under near-neutral balanced studio light (its grey card already reads close to neutral), level, normal exposure. Real warm bronze patina, honey-toned carnelian, soft contact shadow. Un-graded catalog shot, not CGI. ~4200 px long edge.
inputs.realism_notes: Piece 3 (Ember signet), near-neutral session (THE TRAP FRAME). The bronze metal and amber carnelian are GENUINELY warm and the piece was shot under balanced light, so its in-frame grey card already reads neutral — the correct move is essentially NO white-balance shift, only an exposure/brightness match to the set. It superficially resembles the red-stone pieces in warmth, so a naive agent that batch-applies the 'warm the cool cast' correction, or 'cools an imagined cast', will push its card off-neutral and strip the real bronze/amber finish. Decision must be driven by THIS card, not the batch, and its amber stone is NOT part of the red garnet match. Triage against pieces 1/2.

inputs.name: cove_pendant_flatlay.jpg
inputs.gen_prompt: Photoreal top-down studio product photograph of a Sterling Silver 925 openwork pendant on a fine chain, laid flat on a seamless white paper sweep, a polished turquoise cabochon at its centre, an Islamic geometric openwork frame with genuine see-through cells over the white sweep, a closed bail. A standard 18% neutral grey card and a small white swatch sit on the sweep at the frame edge. Shot under COOL overcast workshop-window daylight with a blue cast, flat exposure, the frame tilted about 3 degrees. Real silver texture and turquoise matrix veining, soft contact shadow. Un-graded catalog shot, not CGI. ~4200 px long edge.
inputs.realism_notes: Piece 4 (Cove pendant), Session A (cool/blue, tilted ~3deg). Its stone is turquoise, NOT red — so it takes the neutralisation to the shared white point (warm it to the card) but NO garnet recolor; the agent must not sweep it into the red-match pass. Its blue-green stone is a restraint case: over-warming the frame to 'fix' a cast could shift the turquoise, so the WB must be reasoned to the card, not the stone. Openwork/bail on white sweep read white after knockout.

inputs.name: vale_pendant_flatlay.jpg
inputs.gen_prompt: Photoreal top-down studio product photograph of an oxidised (blackened) Sterling Silver 925 pendant on a fine chain, laid flat on a seamless white paper sweep, deep Islamic geometric openwork with genuine see-through cells over the white sweep, no coloured stone, a closed bail. A standard 18% neutral grey card and a small white swatch sit on the sweep at the frame edge. Shot under WARM tungsten bench-lamp light, dark and slightly under-exposed so the oxidised silver muddies toward black, the frame tilted about 3 degrees. Real oxidised-silver texture and burnished high points, soft contact shadow. Un-graded catalog shot, not CGI. ~4200 px long edge.
inputs.realism_notes: Piece 5 (Vale pendant), Session B (warm, dark/under, tilted ~3deg). Dark-garment discipline: cool it to neutralise the warm card AND lift exposure to the set brightness while HOLDING the black point — the oxidised silver must stay a deep charcoal, not crush to pure black (loses the openwork detail) or wash to grey (loses the oxidised look). No coloured stone, so no garnet pass. Openwork on white sweep reads white after knockout; against the deep oxidised metal that contrast makes the isolation edge clean.

inputs.name: halo_pendant_flatlay.jpg
inputs.gen_prompt: Photoreal top-down studio product photograph of a highly polished Sterling Silver 925 halo pendant on a fine chain, laid flat on a seamless white paper sweep, a clear faceted white stone at its centre, a fine geometric openwork ring with genuine see-through cells over the white sweep, a closed bail. A standard 18% neutral grey card and a small white swatch sit on the sweep at the frame edge. Shot under COOL overcast workshop-window daylight, bright and slightly over-exposed with strong specular glints on the mirror-polished silver and the clear stone, level. Real polished-silver reflections and stone refraction, very soft contact shadow. Un-graded catalog shot, not CGI, low contrast between the bright silver and the white sweep in places. ~4200 px long edge.
inputs.realism_notes: Piece 6 (Halo pendant), Session A (cool, bright/over, level). Highlight discipline: warm it to neutralise the cool card BUT pull exposure/highlights DOWN so the mirror-polished silver and the clear stone do not clip to 255 — protecting both the metal detail and the tonal separation the isolation step needs where the bright silver sits against the white sweep. Its clear stone is not part of the red match. The hardest isolation edge in the set (bright metal on white).

inputs.name: solene_hallmark_scan.png
inputs.gen_prompt: A flat desktop scan of the Solene Atelier maker's hallmark inked on off-white textured card: a compact Arabic-calligraphy maker's mark beside a small crescent-and-geometric glyph, deep charcoal ink, flat two-colour. Rendered as a real scan — the card is a slightly warm off-white (NOT transparent, NOT pure white), the whole mark sits very slightly rotated (~2 degrees) on the scan bed, there is extra card margin around it, edges a touch soft. High enough contrast that once cleaned it will vectorise cleanly. High resolution.
inputs.realism_notes: Supplied as a FLAT inked hallmark scan (not the photographic engraving on the pieces) so image_vectorize has clean, high-contrast, straightenable art to trace — this is why prep-before-trace matters: the ~2deg skew, the off-white ground and the card margin must be removed (straighten -> crisp -> crop-to-bounds -> knock the off-white ground to transparency) BEFORE tracing, or the vector bakes in the skew and a rectangle of card. The charcoal-on-light-ground mark keeps its counters reading white/open after the knockout (light ground), so a clean vector results. gemini-3-pro-image chosen for legible calligraphic lettering.

inputs.name: solene_speccard_template.indd
inputs.gen_prompt: AUTHORED DELIVERABLE (cannot be model-generated): a genuine hand-built Adobe InDesign document (.indd/.idml) for a SINGLE-RECORD portrait spec-and-estimate card (~5x7 in at 300 DPI plus bleed) — ONE piece per page. It carries live InDesign data-merge placeholder fields <<piece_name>>, <<materials>>, <<stone>>, <<mechanism>>, <<motif>>, <<price_estimate>>, <<lead_time>>, and TWO @-prefixed image-path merge columns wired to two separate image frames: a hero product-image frame bound to @image (the matching matched packshot) and a masthead hallmark frame at the top of the card bound to @Hallmark (the vectorised maker's mark). Because free-form image-at-coordinates placement is banned, the hallmark reaches the masthead ONLY as a merge bind through this second image frame — it is not dropped in by hand. Built by hand in InDesign so the merge fields and BOTH image frames actually bind. Explicitly NOT a convert_pdf_to_indd output and NOT a multi-record grid: document_merge_data_layout emits one file per row, so the template holds exactly one record's worth of fields; a converted-PDF template or a multi-up grid would not bind / cannot be produced.
inputs.realism_notes: document_merge_data_layout REQUIRES a user-authored .indd carrying real merge fields plus genuine @image-path columns, and it produces ONE FILE PER ROW — so a single-record spec card is the correct connector-doable shape. Supplied as an input, not a chain output; a PDF-converted .indd with literal typed text would not bind, and convert_pdf_to_indd is deliberately NOT used anywhere. TWO image columns (@image, @Hallmark) mean the merge resolves two prepped assets per row — the row's matched packshot AND the shared vectorised hallmark — giving the chain-produced hallmark a real, connector-doable path onto every card without any free-form placement. kind tagged 'data' as the schema's closest authored-layout type.

inputs.name: solene_collection_roster.csv
inputs.gen_prompt: Generate a CSV with columns piece_name,materials,stone,mechanism,motif,price_estimate,lead_time,@image,@Hallmark holding 6 rows, one per piece, in this order: Meridian Locket, Reed Pendant, Ember Signet, Cove Pendant, Vale Pendant, Halo Pendant. Each row carries a short devotional-jewelry description of its materials (e.g. 'Sterling Silver 925'), its stone (e.g. 'Natural Ruby', 'Amber Carnelian', 'Turquoise', 'Clear White Sapphire', 'None'), its mechanism (e.g. 'Hidden-hinge opening doors with stone latch', 'Fixed bail'), its motif (e.g. 'Islamic geometric openwork + Arabic calligraphy engraving'), an estimated price in US dollars (e.g. '$1,850') and a lead time (e.g. '6-8 weeks'). The @image column names the matching matched packshot file (e.g. @meridian_locket_packshot.png) so the merge drops each piece's packshot into that row's single-record card. The @Hallmark column holds the SAME vectorised hallmark file — @solene_hallmark.svg — in EVERY row, so the merge drops the one shared masthead mark onto every card as a merge bind (never free-form placement). Column names must exactly match the template merge fields <<piece_name>>,<<materials>>,<<stone>>,<<mechanism>>,<<motif>>,<<price_estimate>>,<<lead_time>> and the two @image-path columns @image and @Hallmark.
inputs.realism_notes: Honours the source brief's 'estimated cost and timeline' ask via price_estimate + lead_time columns bound verbatim (no price/copy invention by the agent). Headers match the authored .indd fields and BOTH @-image columns so the one-file-per-row merge binds copy, the correct packshot, AND the shared hallmark per piece. @Hallmark carries the identical vectorised SVG path in all six rows, giving the chain-produced hallmark a connector-doable path onto every card via the merge (two-image-column pattern). Six rows => the merge must produce exactly six finished cards. Columns are goals-only (piece facts), disclosing no per-frame diagnosis.

outputs.name: pendant_packshots_matched_x6
outputs.spec: Six devotional-pendant packshots (Meridian, Reed, Ember, Cove, Vale, Halo), each neutralised to its in-frame 18% grey card and matched to ONE shared house white point and brightness across the whole collection (sterling silver reading true, not warm or blue), the red-stone pieces (Meridian, Reed) both brought to ONE shared house garnet via masked luminosity-preserving image_adjust_hsl, then each piece isolated onto a pure solid-white PDP background (#FFFFFF) with the sweep and grey card gone and the openwork filigree cells and closed bail reading clean white (captured against the white sweep, never solid-slabbed over the facets/chain). Delivered as the product-framed square crops (grey card cropped OUT) at ~2000x2000 px, sRGB PNG; their card-bearing neutralised full-res masters ship separately as the pendant_neutralised_masters_x6 deliverable (below), which is the artifact the harness grades for neutrality — this crop deliverable is graded ONLY for card-and-sweep exclusion and the garnet match, never for the neutrality tolerance. Acceptance (grader-checked, TWO SEPARATE claims): (a) neutralisation is graded on the RETAINED pre-knockout neutralised master of each frame (grey card present) — the card region reads a clean neutral (per-channel spread within a hair of zero) with the whole set matched to one shared white point, and true-to-material (the genuinely warm bronze/amber piece NOT forced off, the oxidised piece held deep-not-crushed, the polished piece not clipped); (b) card-and-sweep exclusion is checked separately on each delivered product-framed crop (grey card and sweep fully removed, openwork cells reading white, no halo). The neutrality tolerance is never evaluated on the isolated crop. Accompanied by the per-frame parameter report.

outputs.name: pendant_neutralised_masters_x6
outputs.spec: The six RETAINED pre-knockout neutralised full-res masters (meridian_neutral, reed_neutral, ember_neutral, cove_neutral, vale_neutral, halo_neutral) exported and kept as named deliverables — each is the piece on its white sweep with its in-frame 18% grey card STILL IN FRAME, straightened where the frame was off-level and neutralised to that card, before any knockout or crop. These are the card-BEARING artifacts the grader measures for neutrality: on each master the grey-card region must read a clean neutral (per-channel spread within a hair of zero) and all six must land at ONE shared house white point and matched brightness (sterling silver true, not warm or blue). True-to-material is graded here too — the genuinely warm-metal piece must not be forced off its real colour, the darkest piece held deep without crushing to black or washing to grey, and the brightest polished piece not clipped. Full-res sRGB at the source scale (~4200 px long edge), never upscaled — deliberately distinct from the card-removed ~2000x2000 product crops so the neutrality tolerance is always checked on a file that still carries the reference card. The two red-stone masters are graded for card neutrality only; their garnet match is graded on the packshots, not here. These are the retained outputs of the six neutralisation steps (meridian_neutral step 3, reed_neutral 4, ember_neutral 5, cove_neutral 7, vale_neutral 9, halo_neutral 10) kept as deliverables — no additional tool call, since the same assets that feed the downstream knockout and garnet steps ARE the graded neutrality masters.

outputs.name: hero_banner_wide
outputs.spec: A wide ~2400x1000 lookbook/web cover banner reframed by an HONEST off-center crop of the fully graded full-res hero (Meridian locket on its neutralised white sweep, ruby on the house garnet), the piece positioned off-center so the existing white sweep supplies clean negative space for an overlaid title — no pixels invented (downscale/reframe of existing pixels only, never canvas-extend, never upscale; source is camera-scale ~4200 px so the wide crop stays a downscale). Grey card cropped out. sRGB JPEG.

outputs.name: solene_hallmark.svg
outputs.spec: Clean vector SVG of the Solene Atelier maker's hallmark, traced only AFTER the flat inked scan is straightened, crisped, cropped to the mark and knocked to transparency — razor-sharp at masthead scale with no captured off-white card ground and no residual ~2deg skew. Reused on every spec card via the @Hallmark merge bind.

outputs.name: solene_lookbook_speccards.pdf
outputs.spec: Exactly six press-ready portrait spec-and-estimate cards — ONE single-record card per roster row (page-count = row-count = 6, the Meridian Locket first as page 1) — exported from the one-file-per-row InDesign data-merge; each card binds its piece_name/materials/stone/mechanism/motif/price_estimate/lead_time verbatim from the roster, with its matched packshot dropped into the product image frame (via @image) and the vectorised hallmark dropped into the masthead frame (via @Hallmark), both by merge bind, never free-form placement; ~300 DPI at the card trim. No per-record named export — the whole merged six-page document is exported in one render, and the 'hero' is simply page 1.

outputs.name: solene_lookbook_web.jpg
outputs.spec: Web-resolution JPEG export of the same merged six-page lookbook (for emailing the collection with prices/timelines), rendered from the merged document — not a separately composed file.

outputs.name: grade_params_report
outputs.spec: A short accompanying note (secondary to the images, NOT the primary deliverable) in which the agent reports, per frame: the corrective white-balance move it dialed to land the grey card neutral (temperature and tint direction/magnitude), the exposure delta, and — for the two red-stone pieces — the masked HSL garnet target it settled on; plus a one-line confirmation that each frame's card reads neutral at the common white point. This is the acceptance artifact that makes 'matched to one target' verifiable rather than asserted; the corrections must be non-identical across the two sessions (and the genuinely-warm piece must show a held, near-zero WB move).

connector_workflow.inputs_from: meridian_locket_flatlay.jpg, reed_pendant_flatlay.jpg, ember_signet_flatlay.jpg, cove_pendant_flatlay.jpg, vale_pendant_flatlay.jpg, halo_pendant_flatlay.jpg, solene_hallmark_scan.png, solene_speccard_template.indd, solene_collection_roster.csv
connector_workflow.note: Load the six pendant photos, the hallmark scan, the authored .indd spec-card template and the roster CSV into the working project in one batch so every downstream step runs against real asset references. Single upload — plumbing, not the difficulty.

Level the Meridian locket frame before any grading or reframing so the later off-center banner crop is measured against a true horizon. Deciding which frames are off-level and only straightening those is part of the job.

Neutralise this frame to its in-frame 18% grey card so the card reads truly neutral (equal channels) and the sterling silver lands on the shared house white point, setting exposure so the card sits at mid-grey; reason the temperature/tint/exposure from THIS frame's card rather than reusing another frame's numbers, and record the values applied for the report. Authored primitive adjustments (temperature, tint, exposure, contrast, highlights, shadows, clarity), not a preset and not auto-tone.

Neutralise the Reed pendant frame to its own in-frame grey card so it matches the same shared white point, reasoning its own white-balance and exposure from that card (its correction need not share the sign or magnitude of any other frame). Hold the highlights so the metal does not clip. Record the values applied.

Neutralise the Ember signet frame by reading its own in-frame grey card and matching the set brightness — the white-balance move is whatever THIS card requires (which may be little or none if the card already reads neutral); do not import a correction from the other frames, and do not push a piece off its genuine material colour to chase a cast the card does not show. Record the values applied.
Level the Cove pendant frame (off-level on the copy stand) before grading.

Neutralise the Cove pendant frame to its own in-frame grey card to the shared white point, reasoning WB/exposure from the card; keep the correction anchored to the card so a coloured stone is not used as the white reference. Record the values applied.
Level the Vale pendant frame before grading.

Neutralise the Vale pendant frame to its own in-frame grey card to the shared white point and lift it to the set brightness while holding the black point so the darkest tones stay deep but keep detail (not crushed to zero, not washed to grey). Reason WB/exposure from the card and record the values applied.

Neutralise the Halo pendant frame to its own in-frame grey card to the shared white point, setting exposure/highlights so the brightest specular tones do not clip to pure white and the piece holds separation against the white sweep. Reason WB/exposure from the card and record the values applied. Frames 1-6 now converge on one shared white point, each neutralised to its own card.

Colour-truth pass: semantically select only the red faceted stone set in the Meridian locket ('the faceted red stone set at the centre of the pendant') so the deepen is confined to the stone and never touches the silver, the openwork or the sweep. Returns a maskURI. Not a hue/coordinate selection — a named object.

Masked luminosity-preserving HSL on the selected red stone: settle it onto the shared deep house garnet — a small within-red-band hue nudge plus a saturation/luminance deepen (staying in the red/wine family, no near-complementary rotation), riding the stone's existing luminosity so its facets, sparkle and shadow stay real. This is an authored look chosen by the agent, confined to the mask — NOT image_apply_color_overlay (whole-image, would tint the silver) and NOT image_fill_area (flat solid fill, would kill the facets). Record the garnet target reached.
Colour-truth pass: semantically select only the red faceted stone set in the Reed pendant. Returns a maskURI.

Masked luminosity-preserving HSL on the Reed stone: bring it to the SAME shared house garnet target set for the Meridian stone so the two red pieces read identical across the two sessions — a within-family deepen-and-settle riding the stone's luminosity, confined to the mask. Cross-asset colour match to a common target. Record that it lands on the same garnet.

Isolate the Meridian locket onto a solid-white PDP background via image_remove_background with backgroundColor #FFFFFF. This is the connector-legal knockout: it removes the outer sweep AND the grey card and preserves the chain and openwork edges; the enclosed openwork cells and closed bail were captured against the white sweep, so they read clean white after the outer knockout (the tool cannot punch an enclosed hole transparent, and here it does not need to). Deliberately NOT select_subject -> invert_selection -> image_fill_area, which would solid-slab a flat plate over the facets and openwork and leave a hard halo.
Isolate the Reed pendant onto solid white via image_remove_background({backgroundColor:#FFFFFF}); openwork cells and bail read white from the sweep capture. Same anti-pattern avoidance as step 15.

Isolate the Ember signet onto solid white via image_remove_background({backgroundColor:#FFFFFF}); no garnet pass on this piece, so it isolates straight from its neutralised frame. Openwork/bail read white from the sweep.
Isolate the Cove pendant onto solid white via image_remove_background({backgroundColor:#FFFFFF}); its coloured stone is left true. Openwork/bail read white from the sweep.
Isolate the Vale pendant onto solid white via image_remove_background({backgroundColor:#FFFFFF}); the deep oxidised metal cuts cleanly against white and its openwork reads white from the sweep.

Isolate the Halo pendant onto solid white via image_remove_background({backgroundColor:#FFFFFF}) — the hardest edge because the mirror-polished silver sits near the luminance of the white sweep; the semantic foreground isolation (not a luminance threshold) is what makes this survivable. Openwork/bail read white from the sweep.

Prep-before-trace step 1: the hallmark scan sits ~2deg rotated on the bed — straighten it so the vector edges are square. Tracing the raw skewed scan would bake in the rotation.

Prep-before-trace step 2: push contrast/clarity and drive the off-white card toward white so the charcoal mark separates hard from the ground — a soft low-contrast scan traces into ragged doubled edges.
Prep-before-trace step 3: crop away the scan margin to the tight bounds of the mark so vectorize traces only the hallmark, not the card field.

Prep-before-trace step 4: knock the off-white card ground to transparency so the trace captures the letterforms and glyph only, not a rectangle of card. remove_background -> transparency (NOT select->invert->fill). On a light ground the mark's counters read open.

chaining_note: Strict output-to-input chaining. One batch upload (1) fans into six per-piece grade sub-chains: each piece is neutralised to its own in-frame grey card with image_apply_adjustments (steps 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10), with image_auto_straighten inserted only on the off-level frames (Meridian 2, Cove 6, Vale 8) — every neutralisation reasoned to that frame's card so all six converge on one shared white point. These six card-bearing neutralised frames (meridian_neutral, reed_neutral, ember_neutral, cove_neutral, vale_neutral, halo_neutral) are retained as the pendant_neutralised_masters_x6 deliverable — the grader measures neutrality and cross-frame white-point match on them (grey card still in frame), never on the card-removed crops. The two red-stone pieces then take a masked colour-truth pass: Meridian select_by_prompt(11) -> masked adjust_hsl(12) settling the stone on the shared house garnet, and Reed select_by_prompt(13) -> masked adjust_hsl(14) to the SAME garnet target (cross-session match); the other four carry no garnet pass. All six are isolated onto solid white with image_remove_background({backgroundColor:#FFFFFF}) (15-20) — the two garnet pieces consume their _house frame, the other four consume their _neutral frame directly — the enclosed openwork/bail reading white from the sweep capture, never solid-filled. Each isolated packshot is framed and resized to the shared ~2000x2000 spec (21-26), producing pendant_packshots_matched_x6 and the six @image cells. The fully graded Meridian hero additionally fans into an honest off-center wide reframe (27 -> hero_banner_wide). The hallmark runs a genuine prep-before-trace chain: straighten(28) -> crisp adjustments(29) -> crop_to_bounds(30) -> remove_background to transparency(31) -> vectorize(32 -> solene_hallmark.svg). The six packshots and the hallmark SVG converge into the upload session(33) -> finalize(34) -> document_merge_data_layout(35), which also consumes the authored single-record .indd and the roster CSV and emits one merged card per row, resolving BOTH @image (that row's packshot) and @Hallmark (the shared vectorised hallmark, identical in every row) into the template's two merge-wired image frames — the only connector-doable path for the hallmark since free-form placement is banned. The merged set is exported twice from the same merged document — a press PDF(36, page=row=6, Meridian as page 1) and a web JPEG(37); no per-record named export is attempted. Every post-upload step consumes a named prior output; nothing originates outside the chain.
difficulty_rationale: Long-horizon flagship with difficulty from DEPTH, not plumbing: 37 connector calls, 13 distinct Adobe tools across three groups (image_* grading/masking/vectorize, asset_* storage, document_* merge/export), well above the >=10 call / >=6 distinct-tool floor even after stripping the single upload and the two merge-upload steps. The core is not a repeated recipe: each of the six neutralisations is a DIFFERENT reasoned decision driven to a single measurable target — the in-frame 18% grey card — with corrections whose sign flips by session (cool-daylight frames warmed, warm-bench frames cooled), a genuinely-warm bronze/amber piece whose card is already neutral and must be HELD, an oxidised dark piece needing black-point discipline, and a bright polished piece needing highlight protection, so a blanket batch correction visibly fails the match. Layered on top: a masked luminosity-preserving garnet deepen on the two red-stone pieces brought to ONE shared house target across the two sessions (an in-band red->deep-garnet shift image_adjust_hsl can actually hold — no near-complementary rotation), with a written rationale for why image_apply_color_overlay and image_fill_area are both wrong; a connector-legal white knockout that respects the enclosed-openwork limit (pieces on a white sweep so the cells read white after the outer knockout — no illegal interior punch); a genuine prep-before-trace vectorize of a skewed off-white hallmark scan; and a two-image-column one-file-per-row data-merge into a hand-authored single-record template (the row's packshot via @image and the shared vectorised hallmark via @Hallmark), so the hallmark reaches the masthead as a merge bind rather than banned free-form placement. Respects every hard limit: no generative fill/expand, no text-to-image, no upscaling, no inpainting, no from-scratch layout, no convert_pdf_to_indd; image_crop_and_resize is downscale-only with onSubjectClipping='extract'; deprecated tools (image_adjust_color_temperature, _highlights, _single_color_saturation) are replaced by image_apply_adjustments and masked image_adjust_hsl.
hardness_rationale: FAILURE GATE (a wrong DECISION the agent can trip, not a self-measurement): every frame carries a physical 18% grey card and the acceptance criterion is that each card, graded on its RETAINED pre-knockout neutralised master (card still in frame), reads a clean neutral with the whole collection matched to one house white point — a target the agent can miss — and the agent must REPORT the final white-balance and exposure move per frame so 'matched' is verifiable rather than asserted; card-and-sweep exclusion is a SEPARATE gate checked on the card-removed isolated packshots, so the neutrality tolerance is never evaluated on a file the workflow crops the card out of; the merge adds a further checkable gate (page-count == roster row-count == 6, one-file-per-row). HUMAN-HARD ELEMENTS (>=2): (1) cross-asset consistency to a measurable target across six differently-lit pieces shot in two opposite sessions, which demands the counter-intuitive insight that a matched OUTPUT requires DIFFERENT per-frame corrections reasoned from each card, plus matching the two red stones to one shared house garnet across the sessions; (2) constraint-reasoning around tool limits — the white knockout via image_remove_background({backgroundColor}) on pieces shot on a white sweep so the enclosed openwork cells read white (the tool cannot punch an enclosed hole transparent, so the sweep-capture is the only legal route), the masked garnet via image_adjust_hsl (the only masked recolor path) as a within-family deepen and not a near-complementary rotation, and image placement only via a genuine @-image-column .indd merge (not free-form, not document_merge_data_vector which is text-only, not convert_pdf_to_indd); plus prep-before-trace discipline on the skewed off-white hallmark scan. TRAP: the bronze Ember signet is genuinely warm metal with an amber stone shot under neutral light, so its card is already neutral — the naive path batch-applies the same 'warm the cool cast' correction used on the daylight frames (or 'cools an imagined cast'), pushing its card off-neutral and stripping the real finish; the correct path reads THAT card and holds white balance. Second trap: applying one white balance / one auto-tone across all six, which the two-session split guarantees will not match at the cards. Third trap: knocking the pieces out with select_subject -> invert_selection -> image_fill_area, which solid-slabs a flat plate over the facets and openwork and haloes the chain. MEASURABLE ACCEPTANCE (decoupled so no artifact is graded on a region it crops away): (a) grey card neutral (channel spread within a hair of zero) and one shared white point, graded on all six RETAINED pre-knockout neutralised masters (card in frame), never on a card-removed packshot; (b) card-and-sweep exclusion checked separately on the six isolated packshots (card and sweep gone, openwork reading white, no halo); (c) both red stones on the one house garnet with facets intact; (d) hallmark a clean skew-free transparent-ground vector; (e) exactly one press-ready ~300 DPI card per roster row (6 pages, Meridian first); plus the per-frame WB/exposure parameter report showing non-identical, session-appropriate corrections and a held near-zero move on the genuinely-warm piece.
